title: Inorganic Chemistry III
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Inorganic Chemistry III curriculum: deeper main-group (s- and p-block) descriptive chemistry, acid-base theories (Lewis, HSAB), inorganic redox chemistry, solid-state/crystal structures, and an introduction to organometallic and nuclear chemistry. Coordination/complex-ion theory (crystal field theory, isomerism, nomenclature) is deliberately left to the dedicated CHM304 Coordination Chemistry course.

questions.question: Across Period 3 of the periodic table, atomic radius generally:
options: Increases from Na to Ar
Decreases from Na to Ar due to increasing effective nuclear charge
Stays constant
Increases then sharply decreases at Al
questions.correct_answer: Decreases from Na to Ar due to increasing effective nuclear charge
questions.explanation: As protons are added across a period, electrons enter the same shell, so increasing effective nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, shrinking atomic radius.

questions.question: The 'diagonal relationship' in the periodic table refers to the similarity in properties between:
options: Elements in the same group
An element and the one diagonally below-right of it in the next period (e.g. Li and Mg, Be and Al)
Elements in the same period
Noble gases only
questions.correct_answer: An element and the one diagonally below-right of it in the next period (e.g. Li and Mg, Be and Al)
questions.explanation: Diagonal relationships arise because similar charge/size ratios (polarising power) occur diagonally, e.g. Li resembles Mg and Be resembles Al more than their own group neighbours.

questions.question: Boron characteristically forms electron-deficient compounds such as BH3 and B2H6 because:
options: Boron has more than eight valence electrons available
Boron has only three valence electrons, so its simple compounds have fewer than eight electrons around it and it forms bridging bonds to compensate
Boron cannot form covalent bonds
Boron always exists as a monatomic gas
questions.correct_answer: Boron has only three valence electrons, so its simple compounds have fewer than eight electrons around it and it forms bridging bonds to compensate
questions.explanation: With only 3 valence electrons, boron trihydride is electron-deficient; diborane (B2H6) compensates via unusual 3-centre-2-electron bridging B-H-B bonds.

questions.question: Silicon differs sharply from carbon in that silicon does NOT readily form stable, extensive Si=Si double bonds or long Si-Si catenated chains, mainly because:
options: Silicon has no valence electrons available for pi bonding
Silicon's larger atomic size gives poor orbital overlap for pi bonding, and weaker Si-Si sigma bonds than C-C bonds
Silicon is a metal
Silicon only exists in the gaseous state
questions.correct_answer: Silicon's larger atomic size gives poor orbital overlap for pi bonding, and weaker Si-Si sigma bonds than C-C bonds
questions.explanation: Silicon's larger 3p orbitals overlap less effectively side-on than carbon's compact 2p orbitals, disfavouring pi bonding, and Si-Si sigma bonds are weaker than C-C, limiting catenation.

questions.question: The general trend in thermal stability of Group 2 (alkaline earth) metal carbonates down the group is that stability:
options: Decreases down the group
Increases down the group, as the larger cation better stabilises the large carbonate anion in the lattice
Is unaffected by cation size
Is highest for beryllium carbonate
questions.correct_answer: Increases down the group, as the larger cation better stabilises the large carbonate anion in the lattice
questions.explanation: Larger cations have lower polarising power (charge density), distorting the carbonate ion less, so their carbonates require higher temperatures to decompose (e.g. BaCO3 is more thermally stable than MgCO3).

questions.question: The Lewis definition of an acid and base is:
options: An acid donates protons; a base accepts protons
An acid accepts an electron pair; a base donates an electron pair
An acid increases [H+]; a base increases [OH-]
An acid and base are defined only in aqueous solution
questions.correct_answer: An acid accepts an electron pair; a base donates an electron pair
questions.explanation: The Lewis definition is the broadest acid-base theory, extending beyond proton transfer to any species that accepts (acid) or donates (base) an electron pair, e.g. BF3 as a Lewis acid.

questions.question: According to Hard-Soft Acid-Base (HSAB) theory, a 'hard' Lewis acid such as Al³⁺ preferentially bonds with:
options: Soft, highly polarisable bases such as I⁻ or S²⁻
Hard bases -- small, non-polarisable, high electronegativity donors such as F⁻ or O²⁻
Only neutral molecules
No particular type of base
questions.correct_answer: Hard bases -- small, non-polarisable, high electronegativity donors such as F⁻ or O²⁻
questions.explanation: HSAB theory (Pearson) predicts hard acids favour hard bases (and soft acids favour soft bases) because their bonding is dominated by similar electrostatic/ionic vs covalent character.

questions.question: In HSAB terms, a 'soft' Lewis acid is typically characterised by:
options: Small ionic radius and high positive charge
Large size, low charge, and high polarisability, e.g. Ag⁺, Hg²⁺, Pt²⁺
Being a strong oxidising agent only
Existing only as a gas
questions.correct_answer: Large size, low charge, and high polarisability, e.g. Ag⁺, Hg²⁺, Pt²⁺
questions.explanation: Soft acids have large, diffuse, easily polarisable electron clouds and form more covalent bonds, typically with soft bases such as I⁻, CN⁻, or S-donors.

questions.question: In an ionic crystal lattice, the coordination number describes:
options: The oxidation state of the central ion
The number of nearest-neighbour ions of opposite charge surrounding a given ion
The number of electrons in the outer shell
The molar mass of the compound
questions.correct_answer: The number of nearest-neighbour ions of opposite charge surrounding a given ion
questions.explanation: Coordination number in a crystal lattice indicates how many oppositely charged ions immediately surround a given ion, determined largely by the radius ratio of cation to anion.

questions.question: The rock salt (NaCl-type) crystal structure has a coordination number of:
questions.explanation: In the NaCl structure, each Na+ ion is octahedrally surrounded by six Cl- ions and vice versa, giving a 6:6 coordination.

questions.question: A Schottky defect in an ionic crystal arises from:
options: An ion moving from its lattice site into an interstitial position, leaving a vacancy
Equal numbers of cation and anion vacancies forming, maintaining electrical neutrality, typically in compounds with similarly-sized ions
The complete melting of the crystal
Substitution of one ion by an impurity of different charge
questions.correct_answer: Equal numbers of cation and anion vacancies forming, maintaining electrical neutrality, typically in compounds with similarly-sized ions
questions.explanation: A Schottky defect is a paired vacancy defect (missing cation and missing anion) common in compounds like NaCl where cation and anion sizes are comparable, preserving overall stoichiometry and neutrality.

questions.question: A Frenkel defect differs from a Schottky defect in that it involves:
options: A smaller ion (usually the cation) displaced from its normal lattice site into an interstitial site, leaving a vacancy behind
Loss of both a cation and anion from the lattice entirely
Only occurring in metallic (non-ionic) crystals
No change in the crystal's density
questions.correct_answer: A smaller ion (usually the cation) displaced from its normal lattice site into an interstitial site, leaving a vacancy behind
questions.explanation: Frenkel defects occur when a small ion migrates into an interstitial space, common in compounds like AgCl or AgBr where the cation is notably smaller than the anion.

questions.question: Metal carbonyl compounds, such as Ni(CO)4, are examples of organometallic chemistry in which CO acts as a ligand that:
options: Only donates electron density to the metal, with no back-donation
Both sigma-donates from carbon's lone pair to the metal and accepts pi back-donation from filled metal d-orbitals into its empty pi* antibonding orbital
Bonds exclusively through oxygen
Cannot bond to zero-oxidation-state metals
questions.correct_answer: Both sigma-donates from carbon's lone pair to the metal and accepts pi back-donation from filled metal d-orbitals into its empty pi* antibonding orbital
questions.explanation: CO is a classic sigma-donor/pi-acceptor ligand; synergic back-bonding strengthens the M-C bond and weakens the C-O bond, which is characteristic of the metal-carbonyl bonding model.

questions.question: The 18-electron rule, used to predict the stability of many organometallic compounds, states that a stable complex tends to have:
options: 18 protons in the metal nucleus
A total valence electron count (metal d-electrons plus electrons donated by ligands) of 18, filling the metal's valence s, p, and d orbitals
18 ligands surrounding the metal
18 unpaired electrons
questions.correct_answer: A total valence electron count (metal d-electrons plus electrons donated by ligands) of 18, filling the metal's valence s, p, and d orbitals
questions.explanation: Analogous to the octet rule, the 18-electron rule reflects that many stable transition-metal organometallic complexes achieve a noble-gas-like configuration using one s, three p, and five d orbitals (total 9 orbitals × 2 electrons = 18).

questions.question: In redox chemistry, the disproportionation reaction of an inorganic species is one in which:
options: Two different elements are oxidised simultaneously
A single species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, forming two different products
No change in oxidation state occurs
Only reduction occurs
questions.correct_answer: A single species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, forming two different products
questions.explanation: Disproportionation is exemplified by Cl2 + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + OCl⁻ + H2O, where chlorine (0) is simultaneously reduced to Cl⁻ (-1) and oxidised to OCl⁻ (+1).

questions.question: The halogens show a general trend in oxidising power down the group (F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2) that is mainly attributed to:
options: Increasing atomic radius and decreasing electron affinity/electronegativity down the group, reducing the tendency to gain an electron
Increasing electronegativity down the group
Decreasing atomic mass down the group
Halogens becoming less reactive due to increased metallic character
questions.correct_answer: Increasing atomic radius and decreasing electron affinity/electronegativity down the group, reducing the tendency to gain an electron
questions.explanation: As atomic size increases down Group 17, the nucleus's pull on an incoming electron weakens, so the ease of reduction (oxidising power) decreases from F2 to I2.

questions.question: Interhalogen compounds such as ClF3 or IF5 form because:
options: Halogens cannot bond to other halogens
The larger, less electronegative halogen can accommodate multiple smaller, more electronegative halogen atoms around it, often with an expanded octet
They are always unstable and cannot be isolated
They only form between identical halogens
questions.correct_answer: The larger, less electronegative halogen can accommodate multiple smaller, more electronegative halogen atoms around it, often with an expanded octet
questions.explanation: Interhalogens form between two different halogens, with the larger, less electronegative atom as the central atom, often adopting an expanded octet (e.g. using d-orbital involvement or hypervalent bonding models) as in ClF3 (T-shaped) or IF7.

questions.question: Radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits an alpha particle results in a daughter nucleus with:
options: Atomic number decreased by 2 and mass number decreased by 4
Atomic number increased by 1, mass number unchanged
Atomic number unchanged, mass number decreased by 2
Atomic number decreased by 4, mass number decreased by 2
questions.correct_answer: Atomic number decreased by 2 and mass number decreased by 4
questions.explanation: An alpha particle (helium nucleus, 2 protons + 2 neutrons) is emitted, so the daughter nucleus loses 2 from atomic number (Z) and 4 from mass number (A).

questions.question: Beta-minus (β⁻) decay of a radioactive nucleus involves conversion of a neutron into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino, which changes the nucleus's:
options: Mass number by -1, atomic number unchanged
Atomic number by +1, mass number unchanged
Atomic number by -1, mass number unchanged
Mass number by +1, atomic number unchanged
questions.correct_answer: Atomic number by +1, mass number unchanged
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron converts to a proton (plus an emitted electron and antineutrino), increasing the atomic number by one while mass number stays the same.

questions.question: Half-life in radioactive decay is defined as:
options: The time for all radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay completely
The time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
The time for the decay rate to double
A fixed value of exactly one year for all isotopes
questions.correct_answer: The time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics, and half-life (t½) is the constant time interval over which the amount of a radioisotope is reduced by half, independent of the starting amount.

questions.question: The 'inert pair effect' explains why heavier p-block elements such as Tl, Pb, and Bi show a preference for oxidation states two units lower than the group's maximum, mainly because:
options: Their ns² electron pair becomes increasingly reluctant to participate in bonding due to poor shielding by filled d/f orbitals and relativistic effects
They have no s electrons at all
Their p electrons are always removed before s electrons
They cannot form any ionic compounds
questions.correct_answer: Their ns² electron pair becomes increasingly reluctant to participate in bonding due to poor shielding by filled d/f orbitals and relativistic effects
questions.explanation: The inert pair effect explains the stability of lower oxidation states (e.g. Tl+, Pb2+, Bi3+) in heavier p-block elements because the ns2 pair is stabilised and less available for bonding.

questions.question: Silicates, the most abundant class of minerals in the Earth's crust, are built from the fundamental structural unit:
options: The SiO4 tetrahedron, with silicon at the centre bonded to four oxygen atoms
The SiO6 octahedron
Discrete Si2 molecules
SiH4 chains
questions.correct_answer: The SiO4 tetrahedron, with silicon at the centre bonded to four oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: All silicate structures -- from isolated ions to sheets and 3D networks -- are built from SiO4 tetrahedra that share corner oxygen atoms in different patterns.

questions.question: Which best describes the general trend in the acidic/basic character of the oxides of Period 3 elements (Na2O to Cl2O7)?
options: All Period 3 oxides are strongly basic
Oxides progress from strongly basic (Na2O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al2O3) to acidic (SiO2, P4O10, SO3, Cl2O7)
All Period 3 oxides are strongly acidic
Basicity increases steadily from Na to Cl
questions.correct_answer: Oxides progress from strongly basic (Na2O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al2O3) to acidic (SiO2, P4O10, SO3, Cl2O7)
questions.explanation: As metallic character decreases across the period, oxide character shifts systematically from basic (ionic metal oxides) through amphoteric to acidic (covalent non-metal oxides).

questions.question: Zeolites are important industrially (e.g. as catalysts and molecular sieves) because they are:
options: Dense, non-porous ionic solids
Microporous crystalline aluminosilicates with well-defined cavities and channels that can selectively trap molecules by size
Pure metallic alloys
Simple binary oxides with no internal structure
questions.correct_answer: Microporous crystalline aluminosilicates with well-defined cavities and channels that can selectively trap molecules by size
questions.explanation: Zeolites' regular porous aluminosilicate frameworks give them uniform pore sizes, making them useful as shape-selective catalysts, ion exchangers, and molecular sieves.

questions.question: Which statement about metallic bonding, relevant to describing metals in inorganic chemistry, is most accurate?
options: Metallic bonding involves fixed, localised electron pairs between two specific atoms
Metallic bonding is described as a lattice of cations in a 'sea' of delocalised valence electrons
Metallic bonding is purely ionic in nature
Metals have no free-moving electrons
questions.correct_answer: Metallic bonding is described as a lattice of cations in a 'sea' of delocalised valence electrons
questions.explanation: The electron-sea model explains metallic properties (conductivity, malleability, lustre) through delocalised valence electrons free to move throughout the metal cation lattice.

questions.question: Noble gas compounds such as XeF2, XeF4, and XeO3 were once thought impossible because of the group's filled valence shell, but they can form because:
options: Xenon has a relatively low ionisation energy for a noble gas, allowing it to be oxidised by strongly electronegative elements like fluorine and oxygen
Xenon has no electrons at all
Fluorine cannot oxidise any element
Xenon gains extra protons when bonding
questions.correct_answer: Xenon has a relatively low ionisation energy for a noble gas, allowing it to be oxidised by strongly electronegative elements like fluorine and oxygen
questions.explanation: Among noble gases, xenon's comparatively low first ionisation energy permits reaction with highly electronegative/oxidising elements, forming genuine covalent compounds like XeF2 and XeF4.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes a covalent network (giant covalent) solid, such as diamond or silicon dioxide, from a molecular solid, such as solid CO2 (dry ice)?
options: Network solids have very high melting points because strong covalent bonds extend throughout the entire lattice, while molecular solids have low melting points because only weak intermolecular forces hold discrete molecules together
Molecular solids always conduct electricity
Network solids are always soft and low-melting
There is no real structural difference between them
questions.correct_answer: Network solids have very high melting points because strong covalent bonds extend throughout the entire lattice, while molecular solids have low melting points because only weak intermolecular forces hold discrete molecules together
questions.explanation: Melting a covalent network solid requires breaking strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice, whereas melting a molecular solid only requires overcoming weak van der Waals or dispersion forces between molecules.

questions.question: Ammonia (NH3) acts as a Lewis base toward BF3 to form the adduct H3N→BF3 primarily because:
options: Nitrogen's lone pair is donated into boron's empty p-orbital
Fluorine donates electrons to nitrogen
Boron donates a proton to nitrogen
The two molecules simply mix without bond formation
questions.correct_answer: Nitrogen's lone pair is donated into boron's empty p-orbital
questions.explanation: BF3 is an electron-deficient Lewis acid with an empty p-orbital on boron; ammonia's lone pair on nitrogen is donated to form a dative (coordinate) covalent bond, completing boron's octet.
